title: What is the difference between margin and markup, and why do candidates mix them up?
description: Margin versus markup explained with worked examples, how to convert between them, and why mixing them up changes a case answer.
hook: Margin and markup both describe profit on a sale, and they are easy to mix up under pressure. The difference is what you divide by. Mixing them up can change a case answer by a lot.
body:
The definitions

  • Margin = profit ÷ price.
  • Markup = profit ÷ cost.

A worked example

A product costs £80 and sells for £100. Profit is £20. Margin: 20 ÷ 100 = 20%. Markup: 20 ÷ 80 = 25%.

Converting between them

  • Markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin). A 20% margin is 0.2 ÷ 0.8 = 25% markup.
  • Margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup). A 50% markup is 0.5 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 33% margin.

Why it matters in a case

A client says it "adds 50% to cost". If you treat that as a 50% margin, you will overstate profit by half: on £1M of sales, a 33% margin is about £333k, not £500k.

A habit to build

Whenever you hear a percentage profit, ask: "Is that on price or on cost?" It takes three seconds and prevents one of the most common maths errors.

The denominator changes the business decision

A café buys an item for £80 and sells it for £100, earning £20 gross profit before other expenses. Gross margin is £20 divided by the £100 selling price, or 20%. Markup is the same £20 divided by the £80 cost, or 25%. The cash profit is identical, but the percentages answer different questions.

Now a client wants a 30% gross margin on an item that costs £70. This means cost must be 70% of the selling price, so the required price is £70 ÷ 0.70 = £100. Adding a 30% markup to cost would produce £91 and a margin of only about 23%. A candidate who confuses the two can badly underprice a product.

Check precisely which costs are included. The £80 may be purchase cost only; delivery, returns, card fees and labour can reduce contribution or operating profit. Do not present gross margin as net profitability. A good case solution defines the relevant margin, calculates the price or cost change, then asks what happens to demand at that price.

Try it aloud: "To earn a 30% gross margin with £70 unit cost, we must sell at £100. We should test whether customers will accept that price and whether variable fulfilment costs change the target." This connects the arithmetic to a real pricing choice.
